issues.legal_issue: Parliament may impose service tax on the service of making a venue available for temporary use for a function, and that levy is not a tax on land merely because the service involves immovable property.
material_facts: Venue owners allowed clients to occupy premises temporarily for official, social, or business functions for consideration.
The statutory definition of the taxable service covered services provided in relation to venue use, including facilities and catering.
The challenge argued that the levy was in substance a tax on land, a matter assigned to the States.
issues.conclusion: The levy on venue-related services was within Parliament’s legislative competence and was not a tax on land. Making premises available temporarily for a function is a service, and associated facilities may also fall within the taxable service.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 246 and the Seventh Schedule, Parliament may legislate under the residuary Entry 97 of List I where no entry in Lists II or III covers the tax. A tax on land under Entry 49 of List II must be directly on land; a tax on an activity or income connected with land is not for that reason a tax on land, as explained in India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu. The service-tax power was recognised in Laghu Udyog Bharati v. Union of India. The nature of a levy is determined by its substance, and incidental overlap with another legislative field does not invalidate it; the distinct aspects of a transaction may be taxed separately, as recognised in Federation of Hotel and Restaurant v. Union of India and the aspect-theory cases. The broad phrases “in relation to” and “including” encompass connected services and facilities, consistently with Doypack Systems Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India and Regional Director, Employees’ State Insurance Corporation v. Highland Coffee Works.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_service_tax: A provider or representative challenged the constitutional validity of a service tax on venue-related activities.
predicates.venue_use_for_functions: A venue owner allowed clients temporary use of immovable property for official, social, or business functions.
predicates.tax_imposed_on_service_activity: The levy applied to charges for services associated with making a venue available, rather than to the mere existence or ownership of land.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a levy on service activity associated with temporary venue use for functions, the levy is within Parliament’s legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: Service tax may apply to the service aspect of catering associated with venue use even when food or drinks are supplied, and measuring the levy by reference to a composite or gross charge does not change the levy into a tax on the sale of goods.
material_facts: Venue providers could also provide catering services, including the supply of food and drinks.
The taxable service included catering rendered in relation to venue use.
The levy was calculated by reference to the gross charge, and an exemption limited the taxable base in qualifying cases where catering was provided.
The challenge relied on the constitutional deeming of certain supplies of food and drink as sales.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional deeming provision concerning supply of food and drink did not prevent a separate service tax on catering services. The levy on the service aspect was valid, and the use of gross charges as a measure did not alter its character.
issues.legal_principle: Article 366(29A)(f) deems the supply of food, drink, and other specified goods to be a sale; it does not deem the accompanying service to be a sale. A sale must otherwise satisfy the established legal concept of sale, as explained in State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co. and the related sale-of-goods cases. The service aspect of catering can be taxed separately from the goods aspect under the aspect theory applied in Federation of Hotel and Restaurant v. Union of India. The measure of a tax does not determine its nature.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns an arrangement that supplies food or drink and includes catering services measured by a composite charge, the service tax on catering remains valid despite the goods supply and composite measure.

issues.legal_issue: The temporary provision of premises for a specified function may itself constitute a taxable service even when the provider supplies no additional facilities or services.
material_facts: A clarification stated that service tax applied when open land or ground was let for an official, social, or business function, even without accompanying or incidental services.
The statutory definition covered services in relation to use of a venue in any manner.
The Court held that making premises available temporarily for a function could itself be a service.
issues.conclusion: Temporary provision of premises for an official, social, or business function may be a taxable service even without additional facilities or services.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory language covering services in relation to venue use “in any manner” is broad enough to include temporary provision of premises itself. The expansive meaning of “in relation to” was explained in Doypack Systems Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, and the word “include” ordinarily enlarges rather than restricts a statutory definition, as explained in Regional Director, Employees’ State Insurance Corporation v. Highland Coffee Works.

predicates.service_tax_scope_dispute: A dispute concerned whether venue-related conduct fell within a service-tax definition.
predicates.premises_temporarily_provided_for_functi: A provider let premises to a client temporarily for an official, social, or business function.
predicates.no_additional_services_provided: The provider supplied no accompanying or incidental facilities or services beyond making the premises available.

issues.definition: When premises are temporarily provided for a function without additional services, the provision may still fall within the taxable-service category.
